EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
In response to the UN Secretary-General’s reform programme, 19 pilot countries, including Zimbabwe, were
selected for the preparation of the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF). The objective
of UNDAF is to achieve greater integration of UN activities both at headquarters and at country levels, while
preserving the special characteristics and distinctiveness of the various UN Funds and Programmes.
The formulation of UNDAF was preceded by the preparation of a Common Country Assessment (CCA)
covering the development situation in Zimbabwe. The CCA provided a succinct analysis of four areas of
concern in Zimbabwe. Regarding human rights, the Government of Zimbabwe has ratified and/or acceded to
the major human rights international instruments. However, the country still faces a number of challenges, 
particularly regarding the rights of children and women. According to the analysis, while democracy and
pluralism are generally endorsed in Zimbabwe, and the Government has taken steps to decentralise authority
and responsibility, most functions still remain with the central authorities. Hence, the issue of stronger
institutional capacity for better governance remains a priority for the country. The CCA also reveals that poverty
is pervasive in Zimbabwe, with 62% of the population poor and 46% very poor. This is to a large extent the
legacy of the colonial government and, as a result, inequity still prevails on such dimensions as race, gender,
geographic location and age. The CCA further identifies unemployment as a critical problem, as 39% of the
population of economically active age are reportedly without paid employment. The situation is even worse for
women, among whom 55% are unemployed. The AIDS epidemic is another serious concern, with 21% of the
population estimated to be infected with the HIV virus. According to the National AIDS Co-ordination
Programme, 600,000 children will have lost their parents by the year 2000.
The UN Country Team continues to have a significant impact on the development effort in Zimbabwe within its
various mandate and specific competence areas. Strong inter-agency collaboration has been evident
particularly regarding poverty alleviation, HIV/AIDS, gender, education, health, governance, human rights, food
security and nutrition, and environment. These collaborative efforts clearly demonstrate the benefits of UN
integration and co-operation at the country level. The experience also indicates that more close consultation is
necessary particularly at the conceptual and programme planning stages. To achieve programmatic synergy the
UN system needs to interact also with bilateral agencies and NGOs.
The UN system has indicated its commitment to tackle the above development challenges in partnership with
the Government and civil society in Zimbabwe. Hence, the UN identified four strategic objectives that provide
an orientation and a framework for coordinated UN system activities in Zimbabwe. These objectives relate to (1)
Human Rights and Governance; (2) Equity and Poverty Reduction; (3) Economy and Employment; and
(4) Population and Basic Social Services. While these strategic objectives are not entirely inclusive of all UN
interventions, they do, however, represent the UN system’s explicit common response. In addition, for the period
1998-2000 the UN Country Team identified the following common initiatives: (1) NGO Capacity Assessment;
(2) Training of Journalists on Development Reporting; (3) Poverty Assessment and Monitoring; (4)
Community-based Initiative on Poverty Reduction; (4) National Economic Consultative Forum; and (5)
Information, Education and Communication for HIV/AIDS Prevention.
To facilitate the implementation of UNDAF, the UN Country Team has taken several steps to strengthen the UN
Resident Coordinator System. These include the introduction of a UN Chairperson of the Month on a rotational
basis, the establishment of the UN Inter-Agency Support Unit (UNIASU), and a monthly Administrative Officers’
meeting. Four thematic groups and several working groups have also been set up, covering various sectors and
sub-sectors and drawing their membership from relevant Government institutions, NGOs, donors and civic
organisations.
The document is presented in four sections. Section One captures the UNDAF preparatory process; Section
Two, the national development goals and challenges; Section Three, the Government of Zimbabwe and the UN
system’s response to the development challenges; and Section Four, the UN common support to the national
callings and priorities.vi

1.1 Introduction1.1 Introduction
United Nations collaboration in Zimbabwe is at present undergoing fundamental changes, moving from
individual agency perspectives to a truly UN family concept. The UN has therefore chosen the theme of "Looking
Forward Together" to emphasise its intention for closer collaboration and mutual support in its undertakings.
The present framework for implementation initially covers only a two-year time period. This initial phase will
provide an opportunity to learn to walk together in greater unison in the implementation of the agreed activities.
However, the principles of collaboration and the framework itself will be maintained, and will thereby serve as a
basis for renewed strategies and activities beyond the year 2000.
The concerted efforts of the UN system in making this process of co-operation a success can achieve a
tremendous positive impact on what a united UN can offer to the people of Zimbabwe.
The preparation of UNDAF has seen the fullest collaboration and participation of all United Nations agencies in
Zimbabwe. This document is the result of two inter-agency retreats as well as several meetings and discussions
at various levels. It is intended to provide a long-term vision of the UN in Zimbabwe in its development
assistance programme, in line with the desires and wishes of the Member States of the United Nations and its
governing bodies.
1.2 The Global UNDAF Process and Its Rationale
In his letter of 17 March 1997 to the President of the General Assembly, the UN Secretary-General set out his
ideas for what are called Track-1 Reform Proposals, including those concerning the UN at country level. The
proposals underlined the need for arrangements to secure greater integration of UN activities, both at UN
headquarters and at country level. To achieve this objective, the Secretary-General decided to take several
steps, among which were: strengthening the Resident Coordinator System; preparing a common programme
framework at the country level; and intensifying the drive to establish common premises and common services
arrangements. This was in response to the call of Member States who made clear their wish to see greater
integration of United Nations activities at the country level, nonetheless preserving the special characteristics
and distinctiveness of the various Funds and Programmes.
1.3 UNDAF Process and Participation
The first stage in developing an UNDAF is the formulation of a CCA. The CCA is essentially a needs
assessment tool, whereas UNDAF is a planning tool which seeks to bring together and synchronise the policy
planning and actions of the UN Funds and Programmes. It is a complementary instrument to the Country
Strategy Note (CSN), which is a government document prepared in partnership with the UN. The CSN sets out
a strategic framework for future programming.
In March 1993, the RC suggested to the Government of Zimbabwe the need to prepare a CSN. The
Government responded positively, and in June authorised the National Economic Planning Commission (NEPC)
to lead the preparation of the CSN. In September 1994, the director of the NEPC proposed the outline of the
CSN. In April 1995, UNDP, in collaboration with other agencies, prepared a background paper. However, due to
the introduction of ESAP and the absence of a clear National Medium Term Development Plan, the Government
could not proceed with the development of the CSN, which was postponed indefinitely.
Preparations of the CCA started in early 1997 with the contribution of several UN agencies. These were
subsequently consolidated by an inter-agency working group. The document benefited from an extensive
consultative process involving 18 agencies, and was the subject of a UN retreat held at Kadoma in September
1997. It also draws extensively on UN agencies’ country co-operative frameworks and various Government
reports, such as the Poverty Assessment Study Survey and ZIMPREST.
The preparation of a CCA in Zimbabwe built upon already existing initiatives and on the 1996 decision by the
Joint Consultative Group on Policy (JCGP) partners to harmonise their programming cycles by the year 2000. 
1. THE UNDAF PREPARATION PROCESSZimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page 9
The Zimbabwe CCA is unique in that it extends beyond the mandates and themes of the JCGP group, or UNDG
for that matter, to the entire UN system. 
The Zimbabwe CCA consists of four major components:
• Overview of the development situation in Zimbabwe;
• Broad development issues, i.e. human rights, governance, equity, poverty reduction, economy and
employment, population and social welfare;
• Key cross cutting issues, i.e. children and youth, gender, HIV/AIDS; and
• Specific sectors, i.e. education, health, water and sanitation, agricultural sector, food security and nutrition,
the environment, industry, tourism and infrastructure services.
The CCA set the following priorities for the UN system in Zimbabwe in the years to come:
• Meeting the civic, economic and social rights of all Zimbabweans through better governance and by
achieving growth, which take equity and poverty reduction as the highest priority; and
• Addressing specific challenges to national development, i.e. the HIV/AIDS epidemic, recurrent drought, the
need for social change to achieve gender equity, and reducing threats to the environment.
Zimbabwe is part of the second group of countries selected for the UNDAF exercise. A work plan was agreed
during the Kadoma UN retreat in September, outlining the major steps, dates and responsible parties for the
activities leading up to the finalisation of the document.

1.4 Principles of UNDAF in Relation to Zimbabwe
The following fundamental principles formed the basis for the preparation of UNDAF, which all agencies agreed
to be involved in:
• National capacity strengthening to address the priority development needs of the country, through intensive
collaboration which will promote sustainability and streamlining of existing development processes;
• Involvement of all agencies in the UNDAF preparation, implementation, monitoring and evaluation in a spirit
of close co-operation, team work and synergetic partnerships;
• Establishing systems for enhanced co-ordination, collaboration and complementarity, as well as an
improved structure for information sharing and common databases. The database to support the UNDAF
process will be disaggregated by geographical and/or administrative areas, gender and minority groups to
capture the disparities between gender, districts, and rural/urban areas;Zimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page 10
• While the UNDAF is a UN document, consultation with stakeholders (Government, NGOs, civil society,
private sector, donors etc.) will be undertaken in order to involve them in the UNDAF development process
as closely as possible;
• Improved inter-agency co-operation within the framework of the UN Country Team will be achieved through
thematic and working groups, the latter involving key stakeholders.
1.5 Lessons Learnt in UNDAF Preparation
The following lessons were learnt through the innovative initiatives that the UN Country Team implemented
during 1997 in the preparation of UNDAF:
Lesson 1: For an effective co-ordination at country level, commitment has to come from the top.
Many UN Country Team activities that took place during the year resulted from the personal commitment of the
heads of agencies in the country. Some heads of agencies became so involved in the process that they
personally led a number of activities, such as the preparation of the UN retreat. Such commitment trickled down
to some of the staff, who then became the driving forces for successful co-ordination. The challenge now is to
involve all UN staff and reflect UNDAF activities within their individual work plans. This is because both UNDAF
preparation and its implementation are lengthy and complex processes which require commitment, specific staff
designation and time allocation to the relevant activities.
Lesson 2: For co-ordination to work, UN agencies must have more flexibility in operations at country level.
In some instances, viable and innovative proposals for cost-effective implementation of UN-wide activities have
been hampered by lack of flexibility given to the agencies at the country level.
Lesson 3: To win commitment from all UN agencies, the RC functions have to be owned by all.
Until recently, the UN system activities were seen as being synonymous with UNDP activities. The main
challenge here was to expand the ownership of such activities to other agencies. Explicit measures were
introduced in Zimbabwe to demonstrate that the UN system activities are independent of UNDP operations. The
introduction of a Programme Director concept (the former UNDP DRR), who represents UNDP in the heads of
agencies meetings, ensures that the Resident Coordinator is acting in the interest of the Country Team, not for
UNDP per se. A rotating UN Chairperson of the Month system was introduced to strengthen the sense of
ownership of the Resident Coordinator system among all agencies. The establishment of UNIASU, an
independent secretariat responsible for the UN co-ordination matters, has further enhanced the ownership
balance.
1.6 Costs and Benefits of UNDAF
CostsCosts
• possible loss of agency flexibility and identity;
• common framework may require changes in agencies’ work methods and entail adjustment costs;
• the possibility of a common reporting format for the UN system from HQ to country level;
• setting up and operationalising the framework may require additional expenses;
• possible loss of independence when pooling resources to achieve challenges identified;
• investment to overcome difficulty in getting staff to have a common mission and vision;
• harmonising programme cycles involves substantial costs and commitments.
BenefitsBenefits
• strengthening the UN presence in the country and reflecting a strong image and a sense of unity;
• facilitating Government’s co-operation and work with the UN;
• avoiding duplication and achieving greater impact at lesser cost, specifically by:
having a holistic approach to development;
reducing competition and increasing rational use of resources;
learning from each other and building on best practices; 
facilitating the sharing of information and ideas; 
supporting each other and networking, improving credibility and delivery of services;
• creating the UN Virtual House Information Exchange Network.Zimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page 11
2.1 National Priorities and Key Strategies
In 1991, the Government of Zimbabwe launched the Economic Structural Adjustment Programme (ESAP) in an
attempt to generate sustainable economic growth through a move from the centrally-planned to a marketoriented economy. The launch of ESAP, which was an integral part of the Second Five-Year National
Development Plan (1991-95), was prompted by Government’s concern at the inadequate performance of the
economy during the first decade of independence. Government recognised that the implementation of ESAP
would need to be accompanied by a programme to address the social dimensions of adjustment. It was
expected that the economic reform would initially cause temporary high inflation and an increase in
unemployment. In addition, ESAP was implemented under conditions of highly skewed distribution of income
and wealth and persistent high incidence of poverty, particularly in rural and peri-urban areas.
ESAP has implemented some of its intended policies, particularly with respect to trade liberalisation and
domestic deregulation. The foreign exchange allocation system has been dismantled, price controls have been
removed, investment licensing has been abolished for all but large foreign investments, and the Government
monopoly over the purchase and sale of agricultural commodities has been removed. In order to achieve the
goals of ESAP, a civil service reform was undertaken with the aim of reducing the size of the service and the
concomitant wage bill, and improving management and performance.
However, there are still impediments to achieving sustained economic growth, the most important being the
continuing large fiscal deficit. Government has borrowed around 10 per cent of GDP per annum between 1991-
95. The very restrictive monetary policy that the Government has used to curb inflation pressures induced by its
excessive domestic borrowing has resulted in high interest rates. These have deterred productive domestic
investment, economic growth and employment generation.
The successor programme to ESAP, the Zimbabwe Programme for Economic and Social Transformation
(ZIMPREST 1996-2000) aims to consolidate the progress achieved during ESAP. Government realises that
economic progress cannot be achieved in isolation from social development, and hence ZIMPREST’s key
objectives are “economic growth and social development and greater equity of both opportunities and outcomes
in order to raise incomes and standards of living of all our people, and expand productive employment of rural
peasants and urban workers, especially the former”.
The preparation of ZIMPREST was undertaken within the context of a broader initiative entitled Vision 2020,
which sets out long-term national goals. Vision 2020 gives strategic direction specifically in areas related to
governance, maintenance of political stability and diversification of the economy to achieve high growth rates. It
emphasises the acceleration of rural development and access to social services for all, as well as the issue of
equal opportunities for all and maintaining a vibrant and dynamic cultural value system. Sustainable use of
natural resources and the environment, and the development and utilisation of modern science and technology
are also seen as of paramount importance.
Given the sluggish economic performance and the continued high rates of unemployment experienced during
ESAP, achieving high rates of growth is even more urgent. ZIMPREST requires that the economy grow by 8% to
10% in non-drought years in order to restore per capita income, consumption and employment to 1990 levels at
the start of the next decade.
The following main economic themes of ZIMPREST are aimed at overcoming the immediate constraints to
economic growth and addressing unemployment and poverty:
• urgent restoration of macroeconomic stability (low inflation & interest rates, stable exchange rate)
• facilitating public and private savings and investment;
• pursuing economic empowerment and poverty alleviation by generating opportunities for employment and
encouraging entrepreneurial initiatives;
• investing in human resources development;
• providing a safety net for the disadvantaged.
2. NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT GOALSZimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page 12
The restructuring of Government is considered to be a prerequisite for effectively pursuing these themes. This
includes completing the public enterprise reforms and revitalising the public sector to focus on core business,
achieve greater value for money and enhance responsiveness to community needs.
ZIMPREST also embraces initiatives to ensure socio-political stability through:
• improvements in the quality of democratic institutions;
• the pursuit of good governance;
• the elimination of corruption.
Also, in recognition of the need to address poverty in a more comprehensive manner, the Poverty Alleviation
Action Plan (PAAP) was presented in 1995. The plan aims to target the poorest and to use participatory
processes involving beneficiaries, NGOs and the private sector to identify and initiate income generating and
community development projects. To date, however, Government resources allocated for the PAAP have been
relatively limited.
The Government further developed a National Drought Policy which was used as part of the preparedness plans
to forecast a potential 1997/98 drought. It focused on strengthening institutions working on drought-related
matters and on support for community programmes that aim at enhancing adaptation to drought. This policy is
to be translated into a National Drought Management Plan.
In light of the above, the Government has identified four broad areas of great concern: human rights and
governance, equity and poverty, economic growth and employment, and population and basic social services.
2.2. International Conferences: Implementation and Follow-Up
A large part of the work of the UN refers to different declarations, conferences, and other agreements endorsed
by the Member States. The international community has convened several major conferences which have
committed governments to urgently address some of the most pressing problems facing the world today. Taken
together, these high profile conferences have achieved a global consensus on the priorities for a new
development agenda for the 1990s and beyond. The continuum of conferences represents a remarkable
achievement for the United Nations system. Through the conference process the entire international community
has come together to agree on shared values, goals and strategies to achieve them. This effort shows one of
the United Nations system’s greatest strengths: the ability to move from consciousness-raising to agenda
setting, to agreement on action by Member States to follow up on conference commitments and to provide
effective assistance for the countries that need help in realising their commitments.
Zimbabwe has participated in and subscribed to the global initiatives and declarations organised under the
auspices of the United Nations system. These include:

The Government of Zimbabwe, in its development priorities, has embraced the recommendations of the UN

3.1 Overarching Framework
“ Human rights are integral to the promotion of peace and security, economic prosperity, and social equity. 
Accordingly, the issue of human rights has been designated as cutting across each of the four substantive fields
of the Secretariat’s work programme A major task for the UN, therefore, is to enhance its human rights
programme and fully integrate it into the broad range of the Organisation’s activities. ” (Secretary-General’s
Report: “Renewing the United Nations: A Programme for Reform”.
The role of the UN as guardian of all human rights has been aptly spelt out in the document entitled “Human
Rights - the New Consensus” published in 1994 by UNHCR, which describes what different types of rights
entail, ranging from the rights to food, housing and medical care to the rights to self-determination. The problem,
as noted in the Report, has been the common use of the “term ‘Human Rights’ in a very narrow sense, referring
only to the Civil and Political rights and to exclude from consideration as a matter of rights, fundamental issues
such as the right to food, health, education and social security”. “Stemming in part from the one-sided
interpretation of the term 'Human Rights', the concept of ‘development’ has also come to be regarded as a
human aspiration separate from the achievement of Human Rights, despite the fact that at least half the 30
articles of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights specify Economic, Social and Cultural Rights which
constitute the core of much of the world’s development efforts”.
The work of the UN addresses the very broad mandate of the organisation. The understanding of that mandate
is used to shape the norms that the UN pursues, and these are spelt out as Human Rights. The various areas of
intervention represent the translation of those rights into specific actions. Thus we move from the normative to
the operational level. It follows that the scope of work at the operational level is determined by the breadth of
interpretation of the set of rights relevant for the specific area of intervention.
3.2 Analysis of the Four Major Areas of Intervention
3.2.1 Human Rights and Governance
Human Rights
Zimbabwe has ratified or acceded to the following major human rights international instruments:
• 1949 Conventions and their two 1977 Additional Protocols;
• 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the status of refugees;
• 1967 Protocol of the Geneva Convention;
• 1969 Organisation of African Unity (OAU) Convention governing the specific aspects of the refugee problem
in Africa, which have been incorporated into the 1983 Refugees Act. 
National commitment to human rights has been confirmed through the recent ratification of the following
International Covenants and Conventions:
Year Ratified 
• Convention on the Rights of the Child 1990
• International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights 1991
• International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights 1991
• International Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination 1991
• Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women 1991
Two major Conventions, however, remain unsigned by Zimbabwe:
3. GOVERNMENT OF ZIMBABWE AND UN RESPONSE TO NATIONAL
DEVELOPMENT CHALLENGESZimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page - 14
• Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment
• ILO Convention 138 on minimum age for child labour. 
A number of challenges in the area of human rights still remain for the country. The issue of land, particularly
women’s access to land in the resettlement process, is of continuing concern.
With respect to both children’s and women’s rights, violations occur perhaps most frequently at the level of the
family or the community, where legal or other governmental systems do not reach directly. For example, issues
of inheritance laws and legislation against marital rape are still outstanding. Such violations, however, are
usually the product of social attitudes which influence the behaviour, decision-making and priorities of individuals
and institutions in public as well as private settings.
In reviewing Zimbabwe’s first State Party Report on Child Rights, the Committee on the Rights of the Child
commended specific national efforts to implement these rights. These include steps taken to create awareness
of child rights; efforts to assist victims of child sexual abuse, such as the setting up of victim friendly courts; the
continued sensitisation of the police and the judiciary; and the broadening of the mandate of the Office of the
Ombudsman to include investigation of alleged violations of children’s rights by members of the defence forces,
police and correctional officials. At the same time, the Committee expressed concern over difficulties in ensuring
birth registration for some children, insufficient attention to the best interests of the child in legislation and
practice, persistence of economic and social disparities as well as child labour, and the acceptance in the
legislation of the use of corporal punishment in school and within the family.
Governance
Democracy and pluralism are endorsed in Zimbabwe. The current provisions of the Constitution, however, give
advantages to the ruling party in terms of funding and the nomination of a number of Members of Parliament by
an incumbent President. Of the 150 Members of Parliament, 120 are elected by the popular ballot, while 20,
including 8 Provincial Governors, are nominated by the President and 10 represent the traditional Chiefs in
the country. These provisions constrain pluralism and the expression of divergent views in the legislative body.
Government could promote long term political stability and transparency by revisiting existing governance
arrangements.
Another key concern raised by various civil society organisations is the need to improve the consultative
processes of governance. The judiciary has expressed concerns that the governance arrangements favour the
ruling party. It is felt that a new Constitution, developed through a consultative national process, could both

3.2.2 Equity and Poverty Reduction
Poverty is often narrowly defined in terms of income. However, there are many other facets of poverty which
affect the quality of people’s lives, including deprivation of basic services, knowledge, years of life, and basic
human rights.
The distribution of income and wealth in Zimbabwe is highly skewed. The colonial system left behind a dualistic
economy, which discriminates against the indigenous population in the allocation of resources. Unfortunately,
the conditions of the pre-independence era have not changed significantly for the vast majority of the population
of African descent. Zimbabwe still has a large rural population, which depends on underdeveloped subsistence
agriculture. Hence the impact of agriculture on poverty can not be overestimated. There are growth rate
differentials between sectors, as well as unequal access to resources within those sectors. All these are key
explanatory factors of the gap between the rich and the poor. The World Bank estimates for 1990 indicate that
the expenditure share of the 20% of the population with the lowest income was 4%, while the share of top 20%
was 62.3%. This income gap shows that the country has one of the most unequal income distributions in the
world.
Income distribution disparities are not only found between sectors of the economy or between urban and rural
areas, but also within the urban and rural sub-sectors. In the urban areas, where formal employment has for a
long time been the main source of income, unemployment rates have been rising. It is estimated that there are
approximately 300,000 new entrants into the job market and yet only 16,400 new jobs are created per year.
Among the employed, the growth in the wage bill has been highly skewed in favour of management personnel.
Due to the erosion of the purchasing power of the Zimbabwe dollar, indications are that the number of the
employed poor is increasing. A significant proportion of these is women, for female representation is higher in
low wage non-management jobs.
While the pervasiveness of poverty is well recognised, there is less unanimity on its incidence. The World Bank’s
analysis of data from the 1990/91 Income Consumption and Expenditure Survey suggests that 25% of the
population were poor and 7% very poor. Meanwhile, the Government-led Poverty Assessment Study Survey
(PASS), conducted in 1995, categorises 62% of the population as poor and 46% as very poor. While the two
studies have methodological differences, there is a general agreement that the incidence of income poverty has
risen in the 1990s. Women bear a disproportionate share of poverty and at the same time shoulder an unequal
burden in coping with its effects. Where women contribute significantly to the economy in terms of domestic
services, peasant agriculture, and the informal sector, this contribution is not adequately captured in national
economic statistics.
The PASS analysis showed a higher incidence of poverty in rural areas (75%) than in urban areas (39%). Within
the rural areas the incidence of poverty varied with land use type: 84% of the population in the communal areas
where the majority of the people live, 70% in resettlement and small-scale farming areas, and 57% in large scale
commercial farming areas were classified as poor. Poverty is more common in female than in male-headed
households: 72% and 58% respectively. Unemployment and retrenchment were identified by the poor as the key
causes of poverty (30%), followed by drought (29%), and low pay (12%).
The impact of poverty, regardless of its source, is evidenced by the limited access to basic social services
experienced by poor households. Data from sentinel site surveys show that despite the lower maternity fees in
rural areas, a large proportion (49%) of rural mothers deliver at home and the births are attended by traditional
midwives with limited resources. Approximately 10% of urban mothers travel to rural areas to deliver, despite
complaints of poor services there. Upward of 10% of children under the age of 5 are malnourished, despite the
good harvest in the 1996/97 season; 28% of rural households still use unsafe water for cooking and drinking
purposes; 47% of rural households do not have access to safe sanitation; and approximately 20% of children in
the 13-17 age range are out of school mostly due to unaffordability of school tuition, levy and uniform costs.
Among the children in school, a considerable number are paid for by the Social Development Fund. There has
always been a difference in the dropout rate between boys and girls at secondary school level. Added to that isZimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page - 16
now the increased burden on the girl child as the main caretaker of orphans and AIDS patients in the family. This
has resulted in even earlier dropouts.
3.2.3 Economy and Employment
Economy
Zimbabwe experienced erratic growth during the ESAP implementation period (1991-95). Mainly as a result of
two serious droughts, the country saw two years of negative growth during the 1990s. This, coupled with the
greater impact of adjustment measures on low-income families, has translated into lower living standards for an
increasing portion of the population compared with the late 1980s. Nevertheless, the economy showed strong
signs of recovery in 1996, when GDP growth was recorded at 8.1% of GDP. The key contributor to the positive
economic growth in 1996 was the significant 48.6% increase in agricultural sector output. Indeed, the importance
of agriculture to the national economy cannot be underestimated, in view of its significant impact not only on
GDP, but also on food security and employment. The manufacturing sector, which contributes around 20% of
GDP, grew by 3.6% the same year, after a decline of 13.6% in 1995. The mining sector declined by 0.2% as a
result of a slump in world mineral prices.
Other positive economic indicators in 1996 included a slightly reduced inflation rate. While inflation still continues
to be high at an annualised rate of close to 22%, it is still significantly lower than the annualised rate of 48%
registered in 1992. More importantly, inflation was on a downward trend in 1996, from a high of 28% at the
beginning of the year to 16.4% in December 1996. The falling annualised inflation led to slightly lower interest
rates with positive effects on business recovery and investment. Yet other positive signs included improved
business confidence, the growth of Zimbabwe's stock market (the second highest growth rate in the world), and
increased trade balance amounting to US$ 287 million in 1996 with exports amounting to US$ 2.5 billion and
imports to US $2.213 billion.
The budget deficit, which registered at over 10% of GDP annually in 1991-95, was recorded to have declined to
7.1% (excluding grants) in fiscal year 1996/97. The Ministry of Finance attributes this decline to both an increase
in total revenues, particularly tax revenue, and lower expenditures than originally provisioned for, mainly because
of lower interest on debt caused by a temporary decline in interest rates.
Government measures to cut spending and increase its revenues are underway, even though not yet quite to a
sufficient extent. As real Government spending is being reduced, care needs to be exercised that expenditure
cuts are made in non-productive areas and not in areas that add to the capital of the nation, such as education
and health. The planned public expenditure review is a step in the right direction, as are the fiscal control
measures currently being put in place. Continued fiscal prudence and productive prioritisation of fiscal
expenditures are challenges that the Government will need to take on very seriously in order to create a
conducive environment for investment, employment and growth.
The ZIMPREST document points out that Zimbabwe will get back to the per capita income, consumption, health,
education and employment levels which existed in 1990, pre-ESAP, only if GDP grows at 8-10% per annum in
non-drought years, or an average of 6% p.a. during 1996-2000. While the 1996 growth performance met these
stipulations, the country's vulnerability to drought cannot be underestimated. Achievement of an average annual
economic growth of 6% up till the year 2000 may in fact already be a tall order, since the 1997 growth rate was
only 2.4%, and the current forecast for 1998 GDP growth is 1.4%.
Employment
The rate of unemployment in Zimbabwe is estimated at around 30% by Government and 44% by the Zimbabwe
Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU). Both ZCTU and ILO studies show a declining trend in formal sector
employment growth since independence. Young people aged between 15 and 24 years account for around twothirds of the number of unemployed. The high rate of youth unemployment has serious social and politicalZimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page - 17
implications. Therefore, strategies to tap young people’s potential and involve them in economically productive
activities should be a high development priority.
Between 1981 and 1990, average annual employment growth was registered at 2.7%, while from 1990 through
1996, it was only 0.24%. This declining growth trend is particularly worrisome in view of the high annual growth
of the labour force. The fact that the projected employment response to the economic reform has not yet
occurred, due to limited economic expansion, adds to the social costs of adjustment. The PASS reveals that
unemployment and retrenchment are viewed by the poor as the key causes of poverty, and that 39% of the
population of economically active age is without paid employment. This national average disguises the fact that
55% of women are without paid employment either in the formal or informal sectors, as compared to 32% of
men. National labour statistics reveal that only 20% of those in formal sector employment are women.
Formal non-agricultural employment stood at 912,000 in 1996, compared to 939,800 in 1991. Two sectors have
contributed to a large portion of this decline, manufacturing and the public sector. The decline in the latter is
largely attributable to the civil service reform. Employment in the manufacturing sector has declined from
205,500 employed in 1991 to 184,600 in June 1996. The decline in the manufacturing sector can possibly be
attributed to the fact that ESAP entailed reducing the level of protection to manufacturing industries in order to
enhance competitiveness and productivity. Formal employment in the agricultural sector increased from 304,200
to 328,800 between 1991 and 1996.
The increasing role of the informal sector in providing employment is encouraging. There are now approximately
one million micro- and small-scale enterprises in Zimbabwe, employing 1.56 million people - an increase of 6.2%
since 1993. While the informal sector creates survival opportunities, most of its participants live below the
poverty line and find themselves in a low-productivity and low-profit trap.
3.2.4 Population and Basic Social Services
Following independence, Zimbabwe made great progress in extending services to the population. In 1982 the
Government adopted the Primary Health Care approach as the strategy to redress health inequalities. 
Emphasis was placed on improving preventive care, as well as ensuring access to health care services for all.
The success of these efforts is apparent in the declining mortality and fertility rates throughout the 1980s, as well
as health care coverage and utilisation figures. Nevertheless, a number of key challenges and concerns are
presently recognised by the Government: the emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases (e.g.
tuberculosis) coupled with recurrent economic difficulties, droughts, and the high prevalence of HIV/AIDS. 
These factors have a drastic effect in the ability of the health sector to cope with demand.
Life expectancy at birth in Zimbabwe was calculated at 58 years for males and 62 years for females, according
to the 1992 census. No updated official statistics are yet available. However, the slight increase in child mortality
demonstrated by the 1994 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and high HIV prevalence rates suggest
mortality is increasing while life expectancy is dropping. Zimbabwe appears to be in a relatively early stage of the
AIDS epidemic. It is estimated that 21% of the population of sexually active age is now infected with HIV. Given
the usual incubation period of HIV - 6 to 10 years - and the trends apparent from HIV surveillance data,
increasing mortality rates are expected over the next 10 years, especially among persons aged 20 to 49 years,
as well as among infants and children under 5, if all other conditions remain the same. The National AIDS Coordination Programme estimates some 600,000 children will have lost one or both parents by 2000.
Zimbabwe’s population stood at 10.4 million at the time of the 1992 census, and has risen to around 11.8 million
according to the 1997 intercensal survey. The census reports an annual growth rate of 3.1% for 1982-92. By
1997, the growth rate had fallen to 2.5%. Fertility remained at about 1994 levels, but mortality had increased
dramatically because of AIDS. Unofficial projections which take into account Government HIV/AIDS prevalence
data and which have been calculated by the Blair Research Institute, the United States Bureau of the Census
and the National AIDS Co-ordination Programme, suggest that the annual population growth rate will continue to
fall to between 0 and 1.5% shortly after the year 2000 as mortality among those currently HIV positive
accelerates. Zimbabwe UNDAF – Final Draft – Page - 18
Zimbabwe’s declining population growth rate is the product of several key developments. Following
independence in 1980, investments in education and health, including family planning services, increased. The
1994 DHS documents a decrease in the reported average ideal number of children from 4.9 in 1988 to 4.3 in
1994; a steady increase in knowledge and use of family planning methods, and a decline in total fertility from
over 6 in the early 1980s to 4.3 in 1994. 
Although overall growth may be slowing, some particular aspects of fertility in Zimbabwe still merit attention.
Adolescent fertility, for example, is very high: among all women between 15-19 years, 19.7% have begun
childbearing, a figure that rises to 44.1% among 19 year olds. Government has noted that addressing this issue
should be an important priority; the draft Health Strategy paper stresses that teenage pregnancies, age at first
pregnancy and age at marriage are areas requiring increased attention. 
A demographic issue requiring more attention, at least at the level of research, is urbanisation. Problems
associated with increased urbanisation have been observed over the past decade. These include, among
others, the raising phenomenon of street children, pressure on social services, urban squalor and increase in the
number of urban poor. On the other hand, the majority of the population live in rural areas where there is no
access to basic telecommunication services and are therefore deprived of information which is fundamental for
securing sustainable human development.

3.4. LESSONS LEARNT FROM UN DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE
If the UN system is to respond to the specific and changing needs of the countries in which it operates, the
following constraining factors must be overcome:
• Lack of appropriate consultations at conceptual, programme and planning stages; lack of recognition of
agency roles and mandates, and differences in budget cycles;
• Limitations imposed by individual agency mandates, pre- and post-intervention reporting formats, different
degrees of delegation of authority and decentralisation among agencies;
• Lack of geographical balance in targeting interventions;
• Uncoordinated communication with Government;
• Differences in personnel policies, appraisal systems and administrative policies, rules, regulations and
practices, as well as their interpretation and application;
• Poor information about other agencies and mechanisms for exchange of such information;
• Manpower problems/frequent changes in staff assigned to collaborative activities and/or areas of common
interest;
• Individualised resource mobilisation.
Among the measures necessary to address the above are:
• Respective agencies’ HQs to allocate resources to support in-country inter-agency activities;
• Commitment by heads of agencies has already been established. It is important that all staff members share
the same level of commitment. The concept of UNDAF needs to be marketed to create awareness among
all staff members;
• More supportive mechanisms need to be established at respective headquarters levels;
• Creation of a common UN Desk in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs must be supported.

4.2 Towards a Common UN Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF)
4.2.1 Overall Framework
“The UN has distinct and inherent advantages as an arena for reaching international agreements and adopting
treaties and conventions of a global scope. This is the normative role of the UN, which applies equally to all
member states. However norms cannot be established in a vacuum. They have to be adopted and implemented
by the people and institutions of member states, with or without international operational support.” (The UN in
Development: Strengthening the UN through Change: Fulfilling Its Economic and Social Mandate). The UN
therefore works at two levels. The first level is the establishment of norms and values – a minimum standard.
The second level consists of the operationalisation of those norms and standards through monitoring and
supporting national and local level efforts to attain the standards. Hence, the distinction between the normative
and the operational work of the UN.
Each of the UN agencies in Zimbabwe is responsible for the development, oversight and management of its own
respective country programme. Based on the assessment of the emerging development challenges, and in line
with Government priorities, the United Nations system is committed to tackle these key issues in partnership with
the Government and the civil society of Zimbabwe. The UN system as whole has identified four strategic
objectives that provide an orientation and a framework for co-ordinated UN system activities in Zimbabwe (see
section 4.2.2 below). As a whole, it is estimated that in 1997 the UN system development assistance amounted
to about US$30 million.
While these strategic objectives are not meant to be entirely inclusive of all UN interventions, they do represent
the UN system’s explicit common response. They focus on areas of co-operation which guide interventions to
enhance the relevance and impact of the UN system, thereby strengthening national capacity. Promoting
national ownership, capacity building and participatory processes are the pillars of all UN interventions in
Zimbabwe.

therefore crucial that journalists reporting on development questions understand the complexities involved and

will enhance public participation in various national development efforts.

salaries, deficiencies in the staff grading system, advancement, promotion and career development.
The role of traditional medicine has been acknowledged since independence with the establishment of an
Act (1981) on Traditional Medical Practitioners. An association – Zimbabwe National Traditional Healers
Association (ZINATHA) – was formed and its members are registered. A traditional midwives upgrading
programme was started, and it is still on-going with revision and improvements within the Maternal and
Child Health Programme.
Zimbabwe has a National Drug Policy. Drug selection is based on the essential drug concept, embodied
in the Essential Drug List - EDLIZ (1984). Drug procurement is centralised through the Government
Medical Stores. The Zimbabwe Medicines Control Authority is a corporate body that screens all
manufactured and imported drugs for registration under the Drugs and Allied Substances Control Act. 
The Authority incorporates the former Zimbabwe Regional Drug Control Laboratory, established in 1980
to ensure quality control of drugs. The Zimbabwe Essential Drugs Action Programme (ZEDAP) has dealt
with training in rational drug use, development of treatment modules for health workers, supplies, planning
and management. According to the drug policy, the Government aims at having a drug availability of at
least 90% for all essential drugs and a PHC level at all times (recent reports indicate current level is 75%).
The health sector is one of the first in Zimbabwe to consider steps towards its reform and
decentralisation. It is understood that decentralisation could help lead to increased equity in and access
to health care, as well as more cost-effective services. In view of the shrinking public resources for health
care, Government is planning or has already embarked upon a number of health sector reforms with an
aim to mobilise more funds and improve the resource use. These reforms include for instance a Social
Health Insurance scheme where all members of society are covered and consequently share the financial
implications of illness. At present, private health insurance only covers 5-7% of the population. 
Government has recently granted authority for the MOH/CW to retain fees collected at individual health
facilities instead of sending the money to Treasury. This will provide a stronger incentive to improve the
collection of fees at individual health facilities. The process of decentralisation has already been initiated;
the end-goal is that district councils resume full responsibility for the provision, planning and management
of district health services as well as control over the funds allocated to them. It is expected that a
decentralised health system will improve the efficiency of resource use, management and responsiveness
of government health services. Regulation of the private medical sector is under way in such a way that
the range of options available to patients is increased, the pressure on government health facilities is
relieved and the tendency to excessive cost escalation is reduced. Contracting-out of laundry services,
maintenance, guard service and catering is envisaged to produce substantial savings and improved
productivity.
The President of Zimbabwe has set up a Health Commission to review the extent and role of
Government’s involvement in the provision of health services vis-à-vis the national health priorities. The
Commission was also tasked to examine the entire health delivery system with attention to organisational,
administrative, financial and legislative provisions necessary to provide the essential health delivery
system, review actual organisational capacity and accountability, service quality, human resource
management, as well as some other issues affecting the health sector.
The National Action Committee (NAC), an inter-ministerial body which co-ordinates inputs in the water
and sanitation sector, is preparing a policy paper on the sustainability of water and sanitation
programmes, emphasising the positive experiences with community-based management of rural water
points. A village-based consultative inventory of water and sanitation facilities is used as the basis for
planning of interventions in this area. It is now Government policy to replicate this pilot community-based
maintenance initiative in other districts. Participatory methods are commonly used and are now widely
accepted in the sector. The skills are also being applied in other areas of development. The NAC has8
endorsed the use of participatory methods in hygiene education, which has been included in all district
water supply and sanitation projects.
Education for AllEducation for All
Zimbabwe is seen globally as a leader in the provision of basic education to its population. With a 1995
gross enrolment ratio of 102% and net enrolment rate of 86% the country has effectively attained
universal primary education. However, in order to build on this achievement, a number of issues need to
be addressed, including ensuring the provision of trained teachers and improving retention at primary and
secondary levels in all areas of the country.
Recently, the Government has announced its intention to reform the primary and secondary education
system. The overhaul is intended to build in a greater degree of relevance into the curriculum and overall
system to meet the current needs of the nation. This reform presents an important opportunity to ensure
that, in addition to quality and relevance, issues of access, participation and equity are addressed.
The Government of Zimbabwe has also established a Commission of Enquiry to review the education and
training system and advise on the changes necessary to meet the development challenges of the next
century. The Commission is charged with taking cognisance of the fundamental need to develop a
system that responds to the aspirations of the Zimbabwean people, to the changing socio-economic
environment, to technological advances and the imperatives of globalisation.
Food Security and NutritionFood Security and Nutrition
Most important recent developments in food and nutrition include the designation of 1500 Commercial
Farms for compensatory acquisition to settle small-scale farmers from crowded areas and the steps
taken to formulate the Agricultural Sector Investment Programme (ASIP). The first phase of the latter
involves the formulation and implementation of the Agricultural Sector Management Programme which is
aiming to streamline the Ministry to concentrate on the core functions and shed off the non-core functions
to the private sector and farmer organisations. The development of a National Drought Policy is another
milestone in this area.
The agricultural sector enjoyed impressive growth in the early 1980s, mainly due to reasonable rains and
incentives to the previously smallholder sector. Growth of the sector subsequently stagnated from the
mid-80s due to droughts, supply-side constraints, and marketing and pricing policies favouring
consumers.
There are various systems of nutrition surveillance in Zimbabwe: the National Health Information System
(NHIS), the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), and the Sentinel Surveillance System for SDA
monitoring. The community-based surveys (DHS, SDA) are likely to reflect the true picture of malnutrition
in Zimbabwe more accurately than clinic-based data since the latter tends to be biased (for preventive
health care at least) towards those who are healthy, health-conscious, educated, informed and less poor.
Additional key issues in nutrition include infant and young child feeding practices and maternal nutrition. 
Promotion of breast feeding has been vigorous in Zimbabwe, and cultural support for the practice is also
strong: ZDHS found that 99% of children born in the 3 years preceding the survey had been breast fed at
some time. While there is some concern about early introduction of water and complementary foods,
children between one and three years are those most likely to be affected by malnutrition, suggesting the
need for more attention to weaning and care practices for this age group. Another major concern with
respect to breast feeding is the potential risk of transmission of HIV through breast milk. With regards to
maternal malnutrition, very little information is available, and no initiatives are yet in place to address the
problem.
Micronutrient malnutrition has also received some attention in Zimbabwe. Successful efforts have been
made to reduce iodine deficiency disorders (IDD), which had previously been endemic in some areas. 
The Public Health Act was amended in 1994 to include salt iodination, and monitoring has shown that IDD
are no longer a significant public health problem in the country. Vitamin A deficiency is not considered a
problem in Zimbabwe, as xeropthalmia is rare and no national survey of serum levels has been
conducted. However, there is emerging evidence that even sub-clinical deficiency lowers resistance to9
illness; these levels have not yet been assessed in Zimbabwe. As with Vitamin A, national data on iron
deficiency anaemia (IDA) is not available.
There are several challenges to improving food security, and more broadly the nutritional status of the all
Zimbabweans. Efforts to address the disparities caused by the existing land tenure system, and to
ensure effective coping strategies for drought remain high priorities for the country’s development. While
Government’s success in reducing the health sector related causes of malnutrition in Zimbabwe has been
noted, sustaining and improving on this will require a concerted effort within the context of health sector
reform and continued poverty. Finally, there is a need to follow up on the commitments of the Rome
Declaration on World Food Security which the Government has endorsed.
Environment
There are conflicting views about the merits of policing versus education approaches to natural resources
management. However it is evident that policing measures are ineffective when people, particularly the
poor perceive the benefits of breaking the law as greater than risks of doing so, and that education and
extension programmes are of little value unless the beneficiaries see direct benefit for themselves. 
Attempts to resolve this difference are already being made in the CAMPFIRE programme, which devolves
the management of wildlife resources to the communities. In exchange communities earn revenue from
the commercial wildlife utilisation, leading to strengthening of community resource management
institutions, and contributing to the local economy.10
ANNEX D THE DEMOGRAPHIC IMPACT OF HIV/AIDS
Population Division - Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA)
As part of its research work programme, the United Nations Population Division studies the demographic impact
of AIDS in the world. In its 1998 Revision of world population estimates and projections, special attention is
given to those developing countries which are hardest hit (population of 1 million or more and an adult HIV
prevalence of 2 per cent or more) or, because of their large population size, exhibit a large share of the
developing world’s HIV infections.
Among those countries, 29 are in Sub-Saharan Africa (Benin, Botswana, Burundi, Burkina Faso, Cameroon,
Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Cote d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Gabon,
Guinea Bissau, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, South
Africa, Togo, Uganda, United Republic of Tanzania, Zambia, Zimbabwe), 3 in Asia (Cambodia, India and
Thailand), and 2 in Latin America and the Caribbean (Brazil and Haiti). Of the 30 million persons in the world
currently infected by HIV (UNAIDS, 1997), 26 million (85 per cent) reside in these 34 countries. In addition, 91
per cent of all AIDS deaths in the world have occurred in these 34 countries.
The 1998 Revision shows a devastating toll from AIDS with respect to mortality and population loss. In the 29
hard-hit African countries that are studied, life expectancy at birth is currently estimated at 47 years, 7 years less
than what could have been expected in the absence of AIDS (Figure 1). The demographic impact of AIDS is even
more dramatic when one focuses only on the hardest hit countries. For example, the average life expectancy at
birth in the 9 countries with an adult HIV prevalence of 10 per cent or more is projected to reach 48 years in
1995-2000 whereas it would have reached 58 years in the absence of AIDS, a loss of 10 years. This group
includes Botswana, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, Rwanda, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Yet,
the demographic impact of HIV/AIDS is expected to intensify in the future. By 2010-2015, the average life
expectancy at birth in these countries could be only 47 years (Figure 2). In the absence of AIDS, it would have
been expected to reach 63 years/ This represents 16 years lost to AIDS. However, in none of the 34 countries, is
the population expected to decline because of the AIDS epidemic.
In Botswana, the hardest-hit country, one of every 4 adults is infected by HIV. Life expectancy at birth is
expected to drop from 61 years in 1990-1995 to 47 years in 1995-2000. In the absence of HIV/AIDS, it would
have been expected to reach 65 years in 1990-1995 and 67 years in 1995-2000. Due to the impact of AIDS, life
expectancy is projected to further fall to 41 years by 2000-2005: this is 29 years less than expected in the absence
of HIV/AIDS. Mainly due to the mortality impact, population growth in Botswana has been significantly
reduced. The average annual population growth rate of 3.5 per cent per year in 1980-1985 has fallen to 2.9 per
cent in 1990-1995 and will likely further fall to 1.9 per cent in 1995-2000 and 1.2 per cent in 2000-2005 (Figure
3).
In the absence of AIDS, Botswana’s population would have experienced growth above 2.5 throughout the 1990-
2005 period. Because of the mortality impact of AIDS, Botswana’s population by 2015 is expected to be 20 per
cent smaller than it would have been in the absence of AIDS. Nevertheless, because of high fertility, Botswana’s
population is still expected to nearly double between 1995 and 2050.
In Zimbabwe, the second hardest hit country, one of every five adults is infected. Life expectancy at birth was
estimated at 52 years in 1990-1995 whereas it would have been 61 years in the absence of AIDS. It is projected
to further decrease to 44 years in 1995-2000 and 41 years in 2000-2005. In the absence of AIDS, it would have
been expected to rise to 66 years by 2000-2005. As in Botswana, the demographic impact on population growth
in Zimbabwe has been staggering. Estimated at 3.3 per cent in 1980-1985, the annual growth rate fell to near 2
per cent in 1990-1995 and will likely further fall to 1.4 per cent in 1995-2000 and under 1 per cent in 2000-2005.
In the absence of AIDS, Zimbabwe would have experienced growth of 2.4 per cent per year in 1995-2000 and
probably still be at 2 per cent per year in 2000-2005 (Figure 4). Because of the heavy toll on human lives,
Zimbabwe’s population in 2015 is expected to be 19 per cent lower than it would have been in the absence of the
AIDS epidemic.
The South African epidemic began later than in Zimbabwe. One of every 8 adults was infected by the virus in
1997. Due to the later start, the demographic impact is yet to come. By 1990-1995, life expectancy at birth
(estimated at 59 years) was barely affected by HIV/AIDS. However, projections show that by 2005-2010, 21
years of life expectancy at birth will be lost to AIDS: the level of life expectancy is expected to be just 45 years
against 66 years in the absence of AIDS. Population growth, while remaining positive, is also expected to
decrease faster because of the AIDS epidemic. South Africa’s annual growth rate is expected to decrease from11
1.9 per cent in 1990-1995 to 0.3 per cent by 2005-2010; in the absence of HIV/AIDS, the population growth rate
in 2005-2010 would have been around 1.5 per cent (Figure 5). By 2015, South Africa’s population is expected to
be 16 per cent lower than it would have been in the absence of the AIDS epidemic.12
